title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 119: The Ginkgo Biloba: The Resilient Living Fossil
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 119 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Ginkgo Biloba: The Resilient Living Fossil

Paragraph 1. Recognised by its fan-shaped leaves that turn bright gold each autumn, the ginkgo tree (Ginkgo biloba) is a remarkable botanical survivor. It is the only living member of an ancient group of trees that grew alongside dinosaurs roughly 170 million years ago. While hundreds of related prehistoric plants disappeared during mass extinctions, the ginkgo survived almost unchanged. Modern leaves display the exact same vein patterns found in rock fossils millions of years old, earning it the nickname 'living fossil'.

Paragraph 2. By the seventeenth century, European scientists assumed the ginkgo tree had died out completely. That belief ended in 1691 when German physician Engelbert Kaempfer visited Japan and discovered healthy ginkgo trees growing in the courtyards of old Buddhist monasteries. For centuries, Chinese and Japanese monks had carefully protected the trees as symbols of long life and peace. Monks also valued ginkgo timber for building shrines because the wood resisted fire well during forest blazes.

Paragraph 3. In nature, individual ginkgo trees are strictly either male or female. Unlike pine trees that carry cones, female trees drop soft yellow seeds in pairs each autumn. When the fleshy outer skin decays on the ground, it releases strong acids that smell terribly like sour butter or rotting meat. Consequently, city landscapers avoid planting female ginkgos along pavements and choose cloned male trees grown from small cuttings instead.

Paragraph 4. Individual ginkgo trees regularly live for over a thousand years thanks to impressive natural defences. Special chemicals inside their leaves and wood drive away hungry insects and stop fungal rot and bacterial disease. In addition, deep central roots help the trees stand firm during violent storms, while their cells easily survive heavy city air pollution such as ozone and sulphur gases.

Paragraph 5. The ginkgo's famous toughness was proved on 6 August 1945, when an atomic bomb exploded over Hiroshima in Japan. The blast burned six mature ginkgo trees standing near temples and destroyed surrounding stone buildings. Yet their underground root systems survived unharmed. The very next spring, the scarred trunks grew healthy green buds without any genetic damage. Surprisingly, while millions of cloned ginkgos thrive in cities worldwide, wild populations are critically endangered and survive only in small mountain reserves in China's Zhejiang province.
